title: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning
claim: Splitting representations across fast and slow components lowers post-change error and speeds convergence versus using shared features in continual learning.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, left-to-right, vertical dotted lines marking task changes
description: Two wide line plots sit side by side, sharing the y-axis label RMSVE (0 to 2) and an x-axis of Episodes (0 to about 750). Vertical dotted lines mark task changes roughly every 75 episodes. Panel (a), titled TD Learning (CL), shows three curves: red 'Both' features decays to near zero after every task change, blue 'Order-3' plateaus near 0.75, and green 'Order-1' stays high around 1.0 to 1.5 with a light green shaded band. Panel (b), PT-TD Learning (CL), shows red 'Separate' and blue 'Same' curves. Both spike at each task change and decay toward zero. The red curve starts lower and decays faster. A dashed 'Other' line carries a light blue shaded band. Captions '(a) TD Learning.' and '(b) PT-TD Learning.' sit below. The sawtooth red curves draw the eye first.
caption: Results in 1D chain environment. (a) TD learning using both features results in the lowest RMSVE. (b) The separate variant of PT-TD learning has a lower initial RMSVE following task changes, and its permanent component converges to the correct value after just one task.
abstract: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.
